speechtext:
Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior) moved for leave to introduce Bill
(No. 102) respecting immigration. He said: This Bill, in amendment of the Act which was passed in 1906, is made necessary principally because of changes of condition that have occurred since that time. While the principles of the Act of 1906 are not altered by this Bill, the law is amended in its method of operation to meet the necessity of adopting active exclusion provisions along the international boundary. When the Act of 1906 was introduced, it was framed with a view of dealing with immigrants from overseas. Although it applied to immigrants from across the line, it was especially framed to meet the other conditions. Now, it has become necessary to make similar provision for the exclusion of undesirables along the three thousand miles of frontier between Canada and the United States that we formerly had carried out at the ocean ports. And, as the Act was drawn with a view to applying to the ocean ports, it is necessary that it should be amended in its definitions and operation so as to clearly and definitely provide for the exclusion of undesirables who arrive in Canada by rail or by road. There has also arisen, since the passage of the Act of 1906, the question of Asiatic immigration. And while in that respect the Act does not require much change, still it has been thought advisable to provide for effectively dealing with that class of immigration, not so much bv the introduction of a new principle but to provide specific means for the enforcement of the existing principle. This Bill also provides for relieving the situation as it at present exists in which the government has to exercise an arbitrary authority in the exclusion of immigrants. This Bil1 provides that, under certain circumstances, a board of inquiry shall sit and decide on the merits of the cases brought before it, a record of each case being kept. When the existing law was introduced, it was not expected that there would be such an extensive enforcement of the exclusion provisions, and practically there was no machinery provided-authority was given and under that authority an order issued. This is felt to be an arbitrary method for this country, so it is deemed advisable that machinery should De provided for dealing with these cases, each case to be on record so that its merits may be understood by the public. While that provision is proposed, there is another which I place before the House now as being important. While we provide for a board of inquiry for the consideration of cases of proposed rejection at our ports or at the boundary line, we also make provision that, until an immigrant has been received into Canada-that is to say until he has passed our officers-he is not able to avail him-
- COMMONS
self of tlie protection of the courts. In other words, until a man has actually and legally entered Canada, he is not entitled
to claim the protection of ttie courts of Canada. I state this provision of the Bill clearly and thus early in the proceedings, that its) merits-or demerits-may be understood and every opportunity afforded for discussion. If it does not meet with the approval of the House, of course the Bill can be amended in that particuiar.
That is, if an immigrant is stopped by one of our immigration officers at the border before entering Canada-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He would not have the right to appeal to the courts, but once he passes he is entitled to appeal to the courts. We believe that that is a reasonable and proper provision, and necessary for the better enforcement of the Act. So, while we are making provision on the one hand for a method of inquiry into each case, on the other hand we do not admit the immigrant to the protection of the courts until he has passed that inquiry.
And who; will bear the cost of the appeal to the courts? The immigrant himself?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Provision is made in the ordinary way that if an immigrant appeals to the court he puts up a certain amount for expense, and if the appeal is successful any unexpended balance is returned to him.
Is this the same Bill that was introduced last session?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: To all intents and purposes the same. The provision of which I have just spoken was contained in the Bill of last year. In the interval we have taken advantage of the information gathered, and, we think, have made improvements in the wording of the Bill.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

PUGSLEY moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 103) to amend the Navigable Waters_Protection Act. He said: This Bill, if it becomes law, will repeal sections 4 and 5 of chap. 115 of the Revised Statutes of Canada. Let me read these two sections, after which 1 will state to the House what the changes are which are made by the substitution of the proposed new sections:
4.	No bridge, boom, dam or aboiteau shall be constructed so as to interfere with navigation, unless the site thereof has been approved by Mr OLIVER
the Governor in Council, nor unless such bridge, boom, dam or aboiteau is built and maintained in accordance with plans approved by the Governor in Council.
5.	Any bridge to which this part applies, which is built upon a site not approved by the Governor in Council, or which is not built in accordance with plans so approved, or which, having been so built, is nob maintained in accordance with such plans, may, in so far as the same interferes with navigation, be lawfully removed and destroyed under the authority of the Governor in Council.
It will be seen that section 4 makes provision for bridges, dams, booms, and aboiteau, It is a curious thing that it makes no provision for wharfs or other structures of that nature which might be erected in a navigable water although, by section 2, a work under this chapter is defined to include any bridge, boom, aboiteau, dock, pier, or other structure and the approaches or other works necessary appurtenant thereto. In the drawing of section 4, the work provided for in this section is limited in character to these four classes. Then section 5 curiously is limited to a bridge; it does not even include the other works mentioned in section 4. Another curious feature of these two sections is that they apply only to cases where these works interfere with navigation, and the question naturally arises and has arisen, as to who is to be a judge of what works interfere with navigation. By section 7 it is provided that the local authority, company or person proposing to construct any work in navigable waters, may file his plan and then if the plan is approved of he may proceed with the work.
The change which we propose making in the statutes is to extend the provisions of section 4 so as to include bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau, dock, pier or other structure of any kind. The new section also pro- [DOT] vides that if such a structure is to be erected in a navigable water the plans must be filed and the usual notice given and the application made to the Minister of Public Works.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

RODOLPHE LEMIEUX moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 104) to control the rates and facilities of Ocean Cable Companies, and to amend the Railway Act with respect to Telegraphs and Telephones and the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners. He said:	Briefly this Bill is intended to bring under the control of the Railway Commission the cable companies and also the cable companies operating in

conjunction with the land telegraph lines of Canada. As the subject is rather a complex one I intend to prepare a synopsis of this and the following Bill and send them to the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) and then on the second reading of the two Bills I shall fully explain their purpose. Everybody is aware that the railway companies, the express companies, the telegraph and telephone companies are all placed under the control of the Railway Board and we intend to bring the cable companies also under that control.

speechtext: Will it include Marconi wireless?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT-CONTROL OF CABLE RATES.
speechtext: Yes, I intend to include under this Bill the wireless companies also. When this Act comes into force, the companies will have four months within which to file with the board their tariffs. In case there are difficulties in filing the tariffs that time may be extended but not to a greater time than one year.

From this amount and the interest which the payments have earned at 4 per cent, the sum of $7,103.15 has been paid to immediate annuitants, such payments including a return to the purchaser of a portion of his purchase money. After deducting this sum of $7,103.15, there will be carried to the credit of interest account on the whole fund up to the 31st March, 1910, the sum of $9,563.71. On the orders of the day being called:

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask a question of the right hon. First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), but as I would like to say a few words, perhaps I will be pardoned if I rise to a question of privilege instead, my excuse for doing so being the statement of the right hon. First Minister to me the other day that I was somewhat out of date. It is in regard to the report of the fisheries commission. The right hon. gentleman took exception to my calling it a report, and told me when I called it a report that I was out of date. But the right hon. gentleman, in several parts of his speech, called it a report; so that if I was out of date, he must not make fish of one and fowl of another.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am glad that I was in good company.

I am glad to know that the Prime Minister thinks he was in good company. I estimate it at the same value as himself. He was absolutely out of date, and I will prove it from his own words. He said that the report had been signed by two commissioners and sent to a third for approval and signature. He was absolutely out of date when he said so as he will prove if he lays the report before the House. It is signed by the three commissioners who are existent to-day. There were three commissioners appointed in the first place, one of them resigned because he was appointed to a judgeship, and after the resignation a third commissioner was appointed in the place of the commissioner who had resigned to accept a judgeship. The three commissioners came here together, spent a week or ten days, made a report, presented that report, that repost has been printed, and all I ask is that the report as printed and signed by the three commissioners be brought before the House. May I not suggest to the First Minister that I have a right to ask for that, and that I have a right to have it brought down. It must be authentic if it is signed by the three existing commissioners. When I ask for this report, I want the First Minister to understand that I am not here in a spirit of joshing at all, but that I am here in deadly earnest. This report refers to people in my county. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) last Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
year promised me that he would have those commissioners inquire into matters that are of great interest to some of my constituents. For instance, one man has sent an affidavit to the effect that he worked for the men who had these closed leases granted by this government, and when he wanted to sell his fish to an outside buyer, the government officials forbade him to do so, although the lease holder offered him only $8 per ton while the outside buyer offered $140 per ton. Even at that the lease holder has not paid the man and now owes him $800. This unfortunate position is entirely owing to the interference of the government officials, as otherwise he would have sold to the outside buyer. Will the government protect that man and others who are in the same box? We take the position in the west that Canada is not in a hurry to get rid of her output of fish, she ought not to be in a hurry to deplete her lakes for the benefit of the United States markets. It costs us nothing to keep the fish in those lakes, and I think it is in the interests of the people of Canada, until such time as Canada requires that fish, not to have these lakes depleted. Would the Prime Minister give me the report so that I may see it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
When my hon. friend (Mr. Campbell) the other day charged me with not being up to date I must say that I somewhat resented the imputation. Of course I am an eastern man and I cannot expect to be up to the standard of western men, but I try to be, I do my best, and when the hon. member charged me with not being up to date in the new department which it is my misfortune to administer just now owing to the illness of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, I sent for the papers and looked them over. I found that a commission was appointed consisting of Messrs. Metcalfe, Reid and Professor Prince, the government fishery inspector. They were to investigate the four lakes in Manitoba and the Northwest, Lac du Bonnet, Lake Winnipegosis, Lake Manitoba and Lake Winnipeg. I found a report prepared and ready for publication concerning Lac du Bonnet which was investigated by the three commissioners I have named. I understand that after this report was prepared Mr. Metcalfe was appointed a judge. I have not yet found whether he resigned ,or not, but it was thought that his new duties were not compatible with the exercise of his functions as a judge and a new commissioner was appointed, Mr. Hogg. Mr. Hogg and the two remaining commissioners have been investigating the three other lakes. The report concerning Lac du Bonnet is printed, but the original of it has not been signed by Judge Metcalfe. It has been sent to him for signature. I have looked into the report and can see no rea-

son why it should not be brought down. The same remark applies to the interim reports on the' other lakes. This morning I called on my colleague who, I am glad to say, is better and could talk business, and I suggested to him that I saw no reason why these reports should not be brought down for the satisfaction of my hon. friend and his friends. My colleague saw no reason why the reports should not be brought down and they will be presented to-morrow morning.
Now you are up to date.

I would remind the right hon. leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that on Friday last he promised to give me an answer on Monday as to the report of Professor Prince and Dr. Starr Jordan with regard to the regulations that were being prepared concerning fishing in international waters.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have looked into the matter and I find that the regulations have been made, but there was an agreement that they should be published simultaneously in Washington and Ottawa. We are communicating with Washington now to have them brought down. We are pressing the matter. I sent a new despatch to-day.

I notice in the press that President Taft has issued a proclamation or made known his view with reference to the relation of certain countries to the United States as regards the minimum tariff. Amongst those mentioned as being subject to the minimum tariff is Great Britain. Does the Prime Minister know whether that includes Canada or not? I take it that it does.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I take it so, but I would rather my hon. friend would put the question when the Finance Minister is in his seat.

House again in committee on Bill (No.73) to amend the Interest Act.-Mr. Miller.
On section 1,

When we were in committee to consider this Bill some objection was made to the wording and its consideration was deferred until some amendment might be considered. I have now to move to add this provision:
Provided, however, that nothing in this section contained shall restrict the rights of any mortgagor to repay anv overdue principal 69
or interest, whose rights to pay the same have not been affected by any contract by him entered into.
I think this amendment will get over the difficulties suggested by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley).
I have not been able to look into this. What is the result of the section, when carried?

It provides that overdue principal upon a mortgage may be. repaid at any time by the mortgagor upon giving one month's notice of his intention to pay or bv paying one month's interest by way of bonus.
That is, it nullifies any agreement between the borrower and the lender made at the time the mortgage is given as security, and without consulting the wish or will of the lender?
It provides that he cannot demand more interest in case of the money having been tendered or the notice given.

Is provision made in the Bill to meet the case of a mortgagor giving a month's notice but not fulfilling his notice? I have known that case to occur frequently, and it is a hardship to the mortgagee, who, on receiving notice, makes arrangements to reinvest his money, which arrangement he is prevented from carrying out.
It is not necessary, because it is in the hands of the mortgagee to penalize the defaulting mortgagor. He may, if he chooses, take action to enforce the covenant.
But he may not wish to penalize. He may not wish to throw costs on the mortgagor. At the same time he does not like to be disappointed in making the investment he has promised.
He would be in the same position as though he had taken a mortgage for five years and the mortgagor had notified him, before the maturity of the mortgage, that he would repay it, yet fails to do so.
In other words, two wrongs are to make a right.
I do not think that applies.

I think that if the hon. member. (Mr. Northrup) will read the section carefully, he will find that it provides that the mortgagor must pay or tender as well as give the notice. Therefore, it is in the hands of the mortgagee to accept it or not.

^ It appears to me that this is of very doubtful



benefit to the borrower. It can easily be got around by the mortgagor. As the mortgage becomes due he presses for payment of a renewal. If the mortgagor is not ready to pay, he gives a renewal which costs $5 or $10, and then mortgagee and mortgagor are back in the same position as before. I agree with what has been said by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) that this is a class of legislation very frequently brought before the House and often enacted, but of very little use to the parties whom it is expected to benefit. I think that is the experience of all practitioners.

I am sorry that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Alexander Haggart) was not in his place the other evening when the Bill was under discussion. I think that in practice, when a mortgage matures, if it is permitted to continue in arrears, it must be by the consent of the borrower and the lender. The mortgagee will usually permit the money to remain in arrears until' the time comes when he may call it in and lend it at an advanced rate of interest. He takes the mortgagor at that much of a disadvantage, and the mortgagor must then pay -him the increased rate of interest or go some place else and borrow the money at a higher rate. If the effect of this legislation is to make the parties at the maturity of a mortgage, enter into a renewal agreement, it has the advantage of nutting both parties on an equal footing, and each can take hia chance whether the rates go up or down.
Look at the expense and trouble.

Usually, in practice, there is little or no expense as most of the loan company mortagees, at least in the province of Ontario, are sufficiently willing to retain their investment, to renew the mortgage by agreement without charge. There is sometimes a charge, rarely more than $5 and usually -only $2 or $3.

I move the second reading of this Bill.

This is where we differ a little. This Bill and one from my hon. friend from Montreal (Mr. Martin) and one from my hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) are Bills which materially affect the railway companies, and these companies have requested that the Bills be sent before some committee where the companies can be heard. In the case of the other Bills, with the consent of the promoters they were sent to the Railway Committee where they will be dealt with by special sub-committees. My hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) has two Bills before special committees now. Once these Bills go before the Railway Committee, that committee will appoint a sub-committee to deal with them. Any committee we would select here would probably consist

of members of the Railway Committee. My hon. friend perhaps does not quite understand that there are 180 members on the Railway Committee.

The ground of my objection is this, that the Bill is in the nature of an amendment to a public Act and is; in no sense a private Bill, and therefore should not go to the Railway Committee at all, but go before the Committee of the Whole House in the usual way. I am quite aware that other Bills, perhaps of a similar nature, proposed by hon. gentlemen opposite, have gone to the Railway Committee and thence to special committees, and I believe also that one introduced by the hon. member for Lincoln met the same fate.
And South Toronto.

I do not think that the Bill of my hon. friend from Lincoln went from this House to the Railway Committee with the consent of the mover. If the principle prevails, that amendments to public Bills should come before the Committee of the Whole House, there is no reason for sending this Bill to the Railway Committee. I am quite aware that this Bill affects railway companies and affects them very materially, but it is a Bill of a public character and there is nothing in it to affect one company more than another. It deals simply with the principle of liability, and I do not see how a subcommittee of the Railway Committee is better fitted to deal with it than the Committee of the Whole House. The principle involved is that of liability, and the Committee of the Whole House is clearly the one to discuss a principle of that sort. If it were a question of incorporating or limiting the powers of a company, the case would be different, but that is not the character of the Bill. If this Bill goes to the Railway Committee and then to a subcommittee, it will be likely to be very successfully steered outside of this session. I am very anxious such should not be the case. If the Minister of Railways will consent to the Bill going to the Committee of the Whole, I shall be willing to oblige him and wait until it is called again, but I do not want to be a party to shunting the Bill as it is likely to be if referred to the Railway Committee.

I have no desire to shunt the Bill to one side at all. I have in my make-up a good deal of fairness, and no matter what may be my own opinions, I think that tnose who are to be affected by legislation should be given an opportunity to express their views before we adopt it. Strictly speaking all these 69 i
Bills should go to the Committee of the Whole House, and not to the Committee of Railways or a sub-committee of that body at all; but when those deeply interested say they want an opportunity to be heard, I feel I ought to try and meet their views. My hon. friend from South Toronto has a Bill regarding commutation of tickets, and he consented readily to have it go before the Railway Committee where all parties might be heard. My hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) has one which is largely a legal question, and he arranged with me, before the Bill came up, that it should go to a committee. We had some little difficulty as to the outcome but I said to him, as I say to my hon. friend, that the object was not to detain the measure at all, but rather to expedite it. I do not think that we are in a position to discuss these Bills fairly until we hear the other side.

With regard to the Bills referred to, I heard my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) protest vigorously against his Bill being sent to a committee. The position I take this afternoon is endorsed by my hon. friend. It was he who suggested it. As regards the Bill introduced by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell), it is on a subject of quite a different character. It affects the details of the management of the road regarding which the companies should be heard, but this Bill simply affects the principle of liability of railway companies in the event of loss, which is a matter this House ought to deal with in Committee of the Whole. I do not want the Minister of Railways to take it as an act of discourtesy on my part that I object to the reference to the Railway Committee. I object because I believe that means de lay. I do not believe that the railway companies have any right to be heard on a question of general public policy. I move therefore that the House resolve itself into a Committee of the Whole on the said Bill.
Mr. GRAHAM^ moved in amendment that the Bill be referred to the Standing Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines.
Motion agreed to.

Mr. EDWARDS moved the second reading of Bill (No. 74) to amend the Canada Shipping Act. He said: Mr. Speaker, this is precisely the same Bill that I introduced in the House last session. At that time the Bill was brought down too late to receive the consideration it would other-

wise have received. It is a very simple Bill, its object being merely to place vessel owners of the province of Ontario on a parity with vessel owners of the other provinces with reference to pilotage dues at Montreal. The amendment proposed has been the subject of negotiations between the Ontario government and this government and has also been the. subject of very frequent representations on the part of the Dominion Marine Association which represents practically all the vessel owners on the great lakes. Sec. 477 of the Canada Shipping Act discriminates against Ontario vessels in a manner which I do not think is warranted or justifiable. That section reads as follows, speaking of ships exempt from pilotage dues:
(a)	Ships belonging to His Majesty;
(b)	Ships wholly employed in His Majesty's service, while so employed, the masters of which have been appointed by His Majesty's government, either in the United Kingdom or in Canada;	_
(c)	Ships propelled wholly or in part by steam;
(i)	Employed in trading from port to port in the same province, or
(ii)	Employed in trading between any one or more of the provinces of Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, or Prince Edward Island and any other or others of them, or
(iii) Employed in voyages between any port or ports in the said provinces or any of them and the port of New York, or any port of the United States of America on the Atlantic north of New York, or
(lv.) Employed in voyages between any port in any of the said provinces and any port in Newfoundland, or
(v.) Having a draught when loaded not exceeding 16 feet, and employed exclusively in voyages between any port or ports on Lake Ontario, Lake Erie, Lake Huron, Lake Superior, Lake Michigan, or on any of the waters connecting those lakes and any port or ports on the River St. Lawrence, or between any ports on the River St. Lawrence.
Prior to June, 1908, subsection 5, the last section I have read, granted exemption to vessels with a draught, when loaded, not exceeding 16 feet and employed exclusively in voyages between any port or ports on the Great Lakes and the rivers connecting them and any port or ports on the St. Lawrence or between ports on the St. Lawrence. But this partial exemption was denied by the repeal of that subsection in 1908, while at the same time the vessel owners of Ontario were urging and earnestly asking to be. placed on a parity with those of the other provinces. I ask the House to fairly consider this matter. It is one which affects very large interests. There is hardly a county in the province of Ontario which is not affected by it. certainly every county in the province of Ontario bordering on the St. Lawrence or any of the great lakes, is directly affected by this Act as it now stands. Why should Mr. EDWARDS.
a vessel sailing to Montreal from Halifax or Newfoundland or New York be exempt from compulsory payment of pilotage dues and a vessel from any port on_;any of the great lakes be obliged to pay those dues? It does not seem to me to be fair and I do not think that the Marine Association are asking more than their just rights when they ask that to be changed.
I wish to call attention to by-law 25 of the Montreal Pilotage District. That bylaw reads as follows:
Every vessel liable to compulsory payment of pilotage dues and moved into or out of the limits of the harbour of Montreal or from one point to another within the same, shall pay such dues for the services of a branch pilot, except in the case of vessels which are merely shifting their positions at a wharf and attached thereto by their moorings.
The only vessels that come under that by-law of the Montreal Pilotage District are the vessels of Ontario because all those vessels which are exempt from pilotage dues under the sections which I have read are specifically mentioned as not coming under by-law 25 of the Montreal Pilotage District and consequently that by-law only applies to vessels from Ontario and subjects the owners of vessels of Ontario to an additional tax which vessels from the other provinces are not suDjected to. This is an injustice on the face of it. Ontario vessels, I repeat, only come under section 477 and therefore Ontario vessels are the only ones which come under the provisions of bv-law 25 so they are the only ones subjected to this additional tax. What benefits are received by Ontario vessel owners from this tax? None whatever. Is the liability of the owner lessened? Not in the least. Is the owner's responsibility lessened because he has to pay the tax? Not in the least. Section 474 makes this very clear. That section reads as follows:
Nothing in	this part	shall exempt	anyowner or master of any ship from liability for any	loss	or damage	occasioned by	hisship to	any	person or	property, on	the
ground either of such ship being in the charge of a licensed pilot, or of such loss or damage being occasioned by the act or default of a licensed pilot, or on any other ground.
While	the	Ontario	vessel owner	is
obliged to pay pilotage dues, he may or may not take the pilot on board:	if he
does, the taking on of that pilot does not relieve him from damages which may be caused by his boat even while he has a [DOT] pilot on board. Yet he is obliged to pay these dues from which vessel owners from other provinces are exempt!
Now, when I brought this matter up last session the Minister of Marine and Fish

eries said that an order in council had been passed providing that vessels coming through the Lachine rapids should not be obliged to pay these dues on entering Montreal harbour; he admitted that this did not apply to Ontario vessels passing through the Lachine canal. But I wish to say that the exemption to which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries referred only helped the Richelieu and Ontario boats, and one or two others, and only partly helped even them. But if, as the hon. gentleman say-s, the order in council was passed to meet the serious complaint of the Dominion Marine Association, I would then ask why the repeated protests of that association, representing as they do practically all the vessels on the Great Lakes/ should have been continually ignored? To sum the matter up. It seems to me it is proper to ask: Is there at present a distinct discrimination against Ontario vessels? I do not think any gentleman in this House can dispute the fact that there is a distinct discrimination against Ontario vessels. Secondly, if there is such discrimination, is it just and fair; and thirdly, is not that discrimination not only unfair but un-Canadian, to grant not only to vessel owners of the maritime provinces an exemption which is denied to those of Ontario, but to grant it also to Newfoundland vessels and vessels trading from New England states as far south as New York? It seems to me not only unfair to Ontario vessels but distinctly unpatriotic. I think this is something of which Ontario vessel owners have a right to complain. Large sums of money have been expended in improving the Montreal harbour for the St. Lawrence trade. It is not my purpose to criticise those expenditures, I merely wish to call attention to the fact that a portion of that money, as I may justly claim, has been paid by the people of Ontario. I merely ask what has been asked repeatedly by the Dominion Marine Association, having very large interests in the province of Ontario, that they be placed on a parity with the other provinces in this matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It will strike every one who has listened to the remarks of my hon. friend that if the law has been framed so as to exempt the province of Ontario from the provisions applied to other provinces with regard to pilotage dues, there must have been some reason for it. Looking at the statute, I agree with my hon. friend that one cannot see the reason why Ontario was exempted,- and was not included in the section of the law which he has quoted. The law expressly mentions ships trading between one or more of the provinces- of Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, and mentions no others. As the hon. gentleman has said, Ontario seems
to have been purposely left out in mentioning the provinces-, and it would strike one that there must be some reason for it. The reason, as I understand, is altogether local.
I may be wrong, but it is my apprehension of the facts, that the local conditions rendered it advisable not to apply those provisions to the province of Ontario as they were applied to the other provinces mentioned. I would not, with my imperfect knowledge, presume to contradict the position taken by my hon. friend, nor to express any positive opinion. I think this is a matter deserving of more information than we have at the present time. There is on the face of it, as the hon. gentleman says, an anomaly, and surely there must be some good Teason for such an anomaly appearing in the law. Under the circumstances, I think my hon. friend will see that he would sufficiently advance the cause he has at heart by agreeing .to the second reading of his Bill, and then sending it to the Committee on Marine, where all parties can be heard, and let the matter be threshed out there.

I accept the suggestion of the right hon. gentleman that the Bill be now read a second time and sent to the Committee on Marine. I think the more the matter is looked into the more convinced this House will be that the Bill should go through.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.

GORDON moved the second reading of Bill (No. 85) to amend the Criminal Code. He said:	As I explained on
the introduction of this Bill, it is an exact copy of an amendment which was brought .in during the last session of this House, and which was sent to the Senate on almost the last day of the session; and owing to want of explanation it was thrown out by that body. It is designed to meet the circumstance that very valuable ore, in some case nearly pure silver, has been carried away from the mines at Cobalt, and sold at what are commonly known as ' blind pigs/ where it passes in exchange for drinks. It is sold to parties who make a business of it. When these parties have accumulated a quantity worth while they take it to Toronto and other cities and sell it. The object of this Bill is primarily to put these receivers out of business. If this is done there will be an end to this business. No injustice will be done to any person by putting these receivers out of business because the mine owners do not sell mineral in small quantities. It has been found necessary both in the Transvaal and in Australia to have legislation enacted such as is sought for in this Bill. If the words in the last

line of the Bill ' prove that he came lawfully by the same ' seem too drastic there might be substituted therefor the words ' account satisfactorily for or prove his right to the possession of the same.' If this change is made I submit there should be no danger of the possessor of ore getting into any trouble. It is easy for him to prove where he got the mineral. It was brought up in the Senate that danger might arise to a person for instance a broker who held ore, but I do not think there is any danger in that regard because any broker who has ore in his possession must necessarily know where he got it from or it would be of no use to him. The ore which he has in his possession is no doubt from a person who is interested in a mine, to show what he may expect to get from that property.
I may say that recently what has taken place has proved very conclusively that unless such legislation is passed there is no knowing where the thefts which are now going on at Cobalt may end. While it would be improper to say anything here about the convictions which have recently been made owing to those thefts it might be proper for me to say, to show how valuable some of this ore is, that it was given in evidence in court in Toronto that one party had obtained in one month two tons of ore, and it was shown that this ore was worth $5 per pound; so that, in one month, that party had received $20,000 worth of silver from the Cobalt region. I therefore trust that this House, in its wisdom, will see the advisability of having this legislation enacted.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. AYLESWOETH (Minister of Justice).
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not disposed to take exception to the views which the hon. gentleman has just expressed as to the merit of this legislation. It seems absolutely necessary if any check is to be given to the evil which has been described that legislation of this nature should be passed. This House was of that opinion last session and in passing the legislation in question did so simply from the conviction, as I understood the action of the House, that it would be impossible without it to afford any effective redress in cases or this description. The evil seems certainly serious. It is a crime in respect to which there ought to be prosecution and conviction where there is guilt, and it is practically impossible to secure a conviction, no matter how plain a case, according to ordinary ideas, the evidence may show, simply because it is impossible to identify the particular piece of ore, or any quantity of ore, which may be found in the possession of the person accused, as ore which has come from a particular mine. The difficulty about the matter which was felt in the Senate last year Mr. G. GORDON.
was that it was reversing the well understood rules of criminal procedure as to the burden of proof, and that, instead of putting upon the prosecution the whole burden of proving an accused person guilty, this legislation would require the accused person to prove himself innocent.
No doubt that representation of the effect of this legislation is quite true, but the question is whether that is not justifiable in the particular case in hand and in view of the evil which it is desired to repress. It is not an unknown thing in the course of either a civil case or a criminal prosecution that the burden of proof should rest upon the person who is charged with either responsibility for the payment of damages or responsibility upon a criminal charge. There ,are many instances of it perfectly well known to practitioners in the courts, and apart altogether from instances in which the burden or presumption is at once upon or against the person charged with any particular course of action. it is an every day occurrence in trials that the burden shiits from the one side to the other side according to the special evidence which may from minute to minute or hour to hour in the course of the proceedings be given. That is all that this legislation seeks to do; it puts at the outset the burden upon the person in whose possession the ore is found to account satisfactorily for such possession. That is only another form of stating that the possession of ore, when there is a charge that it is wrongfully in the possession of the person accused, at once puts that person in the position of having a presumption raised against him. In the case of honest possession it will not be a difficult thing to rebut that presumption. Many instances have been suggested where some innocent person might be wrongfully prosecuted if this change in the law were made. It has been said for instance that a mining broker might have samples of quartz or ore in his possession and be unable to state where they came from. That has not occurred to me as any serious difficulty. The presumption which this Act might create if it became law would, in the case of the mining broker, be Te-butted the instant it arose by the circumstance of the character of his business and the fact that in the ordinary course of his business he was just the man who might be expected to be in possession of a great quantity of samples of quartz which he might not be able to identify himself or whose source he could not prove to a demonstration. However, if the phraseology of the Bill is changed, as has been suggested, the mining broker who might otherwise be charged and might be in difficulty under the phraseology of this statute, would at once rebut any prima facie presumption

which the statute would appear to raise by the mere circumstance that that was his ordinary and proper line of business.
Legislation of this character, as the hon. gentleman has stated, has been found necessary in mining communities. We have the example of legislation, not only of South Africa, but also of different states of the Australian commonwealth upon this very subject, at least as severe as anything which is proposed in this legislation. But in our own Criminal Code there are plenty of instances where such a presumption is already created by the existing law and where no evil has come from it. Take any one found in possession of naval or -military stores bearing the broad arrow or marked otherwise as being public property, at once the burden is put on that person of accounting for it satisfactorily. It is but common sense that it should be so, and in the sections of the Criminal Code dealing with evidence at trials many instances of the same sort of thing are to be found. The presence of cards, dice, counters, tables or other implements of gaming affords prima facie evidence that gaming is carried on in the place where they are found. It is but a statutory statement of the deduction and inference which any man exercising ordinary common sense would make in his own mind on finding such a condition of affairs. The finding in an unlicensed house of an unusually large quantity of intoxicating liquor at once affords the presumption that it is there for an unlawful purpose, that it is kept for sale instead of for private consumption. Things of that sort found in legislative enactment, as I have pointed out, simply state in words and by Act of parliament that which is the ordinary inference that any jury would draw from such circumstances if proved before them in evidence. I think, therefore, that this legislation is meritorious. I regret that it was not adopted last year by the Senate, and I support entirely the motion of my hon. friend for the second reading. When the Bill goes to committee I shall propose that it should not extend to or have application in the Yukon territory, simply for the reason that the conditions o,f placer mining _ are quite different from those of quartz mining. In the Yukon at one time, and perhaps still, it was quite the custom to use nuggets of gold, the results of placer mining, as currency. Each man carried his pouch in which he had such gold dust as he had won during the day or week and it passed current by weight and probably does so still. At any rate that is a very different thing. The possession of quartz of greater or less value having possibly a very high percentage of precious metal and in the whole amounting to considerable sums by some person who is not a regular dealer
is something which seems to require to be accounted for and we have already upon our Criminal Code a provision of that character with regard to workmen and labourers. Section 988 of the Criminal Code provides that in any prosecution proceeding or trial for stealing ores or minerals, the possession, contrary to the provision of any law in that behalf, of any smelted gold or silver or any goldbearing quartz or any unsinelted or unmanufactured gold or silver by any operator, workman or labourer actively engaged in or on any mine shall be prima facie evidence that the same has been stolen by him. That has been our law for ten years or more. I do not know that any one has ever found any difficulty from it or been wrongfully prosecuted under it. This legislation is on the same lines and I cannot but think if its effect and the reason for its introduction had been appreciated in the other House, the Bill would not have met with the fate which bqfell it last year.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,
1. The Criminal Code, chanter 146 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, is amended by inserting the following section immediately after section 424:-
424a. Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to two years' imprisonment who, having in his possession or on liis premises with his knowledge any rock, ore, mineral, stone, quartz or other substance containing gold or silver, or any unsmelted, or untreated, or unmanufactured, or parr.ly smelted, partly treated or partly manufactured gold or silver, is unable to prove that he came lawfully by the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think it would be better_ to change the wording. I would suggest The striking out of the words 'is unable to prove that he came lawfully by the same' and substitute 'is unable to account satisfactorily for or prove his right to the possession of the same'. These are the words of the Act of the Transvaal applying to the case of any person found in possession of rough or uncut diamonds, and unable to prove his right to the possession of the same.
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I move that the following be added as subsection 424b:
This Act shall not extend or apply to the Yukon Territory.

I think the amendment would be more effective if it were made simply to exclude placer gold from the operation of the Act. If confined to quartz mining, it will apply to the Yukon as well as to any other part of the Dominion

If my information be correct, there are very rich quartz veins in that territory, which, if not operated, will be operated in the near future, and the necessity of the law will be as great there as anywhere else. As to the Bill affecting the broker, I do not think that would be the case, because the object is to bring to book not only the person in whose possession the ore may be found but the person who sells it. The broker may have considerable samples in his office, but no broker that I know of sella ore.

I think the wording of this amendment should be modified. This is to be included as section 424b and it might be held to relate to the Criminal Code and to exclude it from application to the Yukon. It should be made to read in some such way as this:
The foregoing section shall not extend or apply to the Yukon Territory.
To provide in the Criminal Code that 'this Act shall not extend or apply to the Yukon territory' might lead to confusion.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Section 424 of the Criminal Code is cognate legislation with this which is now being put through the House. It is divided into sub-sections (a), (b), (c) and (d), and the last provides 'the two next preceding subsections' (b) and (c) 'shall not extend or apply to the Yukon territory'.

That is what I say. But I understand that this provision which we are now discussing is to be embodied in the Criminal Code as section 424b. If it were left in the form proposed, it might have the effect of preventing the Criminal Code from having any application to the Yukon territory. It says: 'This Act'-not 'this section'-'shall not extend or apply to the Yukon territory'. That is, according to this amendment, the Criminal Code, shall not apply to the Yukon territory, which would be unfortunate. The words used should be 'the foregoing section',
